entities.name: Critolaus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Critolaus, born in Phaselis around 199 BCE and dying circa 119 BCE, was a prominent Greek Peripatetic philosopher who led the Lyceum in Athens following Lycon. His philosophical contributions centered on an ethical eudaimonism, positing that perfect happiness required not only the goods of the soul but also those of the body and external circumstances. He was a staunch advocate for the eternity of the world and a critical opponent of the burgeoning art of rhetoric, reflecting a deep commitment to rigorous philosophical inquiry over persuasive eloquence.

His most historically significant action was his participation in the famous Athenian embassy to Rome in 155 BCE. Alongside the Academic Carneades and the Stoic Diogenes the Babylonian, Critolaus was dispatched to appeal a hefty fine imposed on Athens by the Sicyonians. During this diplomatic mission, the three philosophers delivered public lectures that captivated and scandalized the Roman elite. Critolaus, in particular, presented arguments for the eternity of the world and critiqued rhetoric, which, while intellectually stimulating, deeply alarmed conservative figures like Cato the Elder, who perceived these foreign philosophical ideas as a threat to Roman moral fiber and traditional values.

The impact of Critolaus's embassy to Rome was profound, accelerating the Hellenization of Roman intellectual life. His philosophical demonstrations, delivered in a city traditionally wary of overt Greek influence, forced Roman society to confront and engage with diverse philosophical traditions. This encounter initiated a vigorous debate within the Roman senatorial class and among intellectuals about the merits and dangers of Greek thought, shaping the intellectual landscape of the late Roman Republic and influencing subsequent generations of Roman thinkers and statesmen.
